contradictions.fact: Whether the 'standard' approach climbs the South Ridge

claims.says: Standard approach for Bulls Tooth: hike south on the PCT from Stevens Pass, then leave the trail near Lake Josephine to drop into Icicle Creek and climb ~1,800 ft into the Chain Lakes basin, then to Bullseye Pass before ascending the south ridge (class 3-4) to the summit.

...The standard line is a Class 2-3 scramble via a ledge system on the west side that gains the ridge crest just below the top; the technical south-ridge (Class 4/5.0) line seen in some trip reports is a harder variant, not the standard way up...

...The final pitch to the top is Class 2-3 scrambling on solid granite; the easiest line works around the right (east/south) side of the summit block rather than the left, finishing with an exposed but short Class 3 step and mantle onto the summit.

No real rack for the standard Class 3 line... Harder direct/technical variations documented nearby (south ridge, west face) go up to sustained 5th class -- well beyond this scramble and requiring a full rock rack; do not confuse them with the standard route.

contradictions.why: One waypoint note calls the South Ridge (class 3-4) part of the 'standard approach', while the route's own beta, approach text, itinerary day-2 note, and detailed_rack all explicitly say the South Ridge is a separate, harder technical variant that is NOT the standard way up (the standard line is a Class 2-3 west-side ledge scramble).
contradictions.internal_resolution: The majority (beta, approach, itinerary note, climbing_route, detailed_rack) agree the standard route avoids the South Ridge; the one waypoint note is the outlier.

contradictions.fact: Whether the standard route requires rappelling

claims.says: ...This is a walk-off/downclimb descent with no rappelling on the standard route: 0 rappels.

...most parties rappel the top section on the way down rather than reversing it, so a rope and a small rack of slings for the anchors belongs on the list even though the outing is graded as a scramble.

contradictions.why: The route's rappels count, descent_text, climbing_route and detailed_rack all agree the standard scramble has zero rappels and needs no rack, but the CAMPING & BIVY entry for Chiwaukum Chain Lakes says 'most parties rappel the top section' and recommends carrying a rope/sling rack for exactly that reason.
contradictions.internal_resolution: rappels/descent_text/climbing_route/detailed_rack are mutually consistent at zero rappels; the bivy note is the outlier.

contradictions.fact: Best/safest month on the Mary Green Glacier (bergschrund/crevasse timing)

claims.says: Roughly late June through mid-July — early enough to avoid heavy snow choking the summit gully, but before the glacier gets too broken up. After about July 20 the Mary Green Glacier typically opens into a heavily crevassed maze that makes the route much harder; some parties still succeed into August/September in low-snow years.
Late July through early September month of August; early-to-mid July can also work in low-snow years for an easier bergschrund crossing
status: optimal, reason: In season; Prime summer, with the driest, most stable glacier and rock conditions
Late-season bergschrund: after about July 20 the Mary Green Glacier typically opens into a maze of crevasses that can end the climb.

contradictions.why: best_season and watch_out both warn that the glacier becomes much harder/crevassed after ~July 20 and treat August as only a low-snow-year exception, while seasonal_guidance calls August the 'optimal'/'Prime' month with no such caveat — opposite guidance about the safest month to cross the bergschrund.
contradictions.internal_resolution: best_season and watch_out agree with each other on the July-20 cutoff; seasonal_guidance's 'August optimal' framing is the outlier.

claims.says: Bonanza Peak is the highest point in the Wenatchee Mountains, a popular mountaineering objective. The North Ridge is the most direct approach to the summit, a straightforward Class 2 scramble over talus and low-angle rock with good routefinding.
From the Middle Fork Snoqualmie trailhead, approach via the alpine meadows to the north ridge base. Follow the ridge crest, staying on solid rock and stable talus.
Stream crossing — Middle Fork crossing can be dangerous high water (June-July); consider trekking poles.
From Ballpark Campground at Holden Village (~3,300 ft), take Railroad Creek Trail (#1240) about 1 mile to its junction with Holden Lake Trail (#1251)...
Holden Village / Ballpark Campground

contradictions.why: overview, beta, and one watch_out entry describe a 'Middle Fork Snoqualmie trailhead' and call Bonanza 'the highest point in the Wenatchee Mountains', while this same route's own approach/waypoints/access/road/bivy fields — and the sibling Mary Green Glacier route on the same peak — consistently describe the real Holden Village/Railroad Creek approach and identify Bonanza as Washington's highest non-volcanic summit and the Chelan County highpoint.
contradictions.internal_resolution: approach, waypoints, access, road, and bivy are mutually consistent on Holden Village/Railroad Creek (and match the sibling Mary Green Glacier route); overview/beta/watch_out look copied from an unrelated route near Middle Fork Snoqualmie.

grade: Class 3-4; notes: Short exposed ridge scramble from the notch to the true summit.

A single rope (or two thin ropes for full-length rappels) plus a standard glacier kit — harness, crampons, ice axe, a few pickets or screws, and prusiks/crevasse-rescue gear... helmet is essential given the loose orthogneiss.

contradictions.internal_resolution: pitch_detail, detailed_rack, the gear list, and descent_text (rappels off slung horns/blocks) all describe Class 3-4 terrain with glacier travel; grade='Class 2' undersells it and is the outlier.
